entry.title: Langhua Jiang: The Storyteller Who Made Chinese History Accessible to Millions
entry.summary: Langhua Jiang, whose real name is Jiang Huajie, is a Chinese history content creator and one of the most distinctive voices in Bilibili's knowledge ecosystem. Born in 1997 in Rizhao, Shandong Province, and currently based in Nanjing, he is a member of the generation that…
entry.content:
Langhua Jiang, whose real name is Jiang Huajie, is a Chinese history content creator and one of the most distinctive voices in Bilibili's knowledge ecosystem. Born in 1997 in Rizhao, Shandong Province, and currently based in Nanjing, he is a member of the generation that Chinese media often refers to as the "post-95s," a cohort that came of age alongside the rise of China's digital platforms. His channel, "Langhua Jiang," which translates roughly to "Waves and Ginger," has accumulated over three million followers across Bilibili and Douyin, with total video views exceeding one hundred million. His self-positioning is deliberately modest: he describes himself not as a historian but as a "storyteller of Chinese history," a phrase that captures both the narrative ambition of his work and his refusal to claim academic authority he does not possess. In less than three years, he has built a body of work that includes series on ancient Chinese daily life, folklore and江湖 culture, and museum artifacts, including a single video lasting four hours and thirteen minutes that surveys all 195 Chinese cultural relics prohibited from overseas exhibition.

Jiang Huajie's path to content creation was neither direct nor instantaneous. Before launching his Bilibili channel in June 2023, he had experimented with WeChat public accounts, podcasts, and vlogs, all without finding a stable audience or a clear creative identity. His breakthrough came with his very first Bilibili upload, a video titled "This Might Be the Best History UP Creator Recommendation on Bilibili," in which he simply recommended other history creators he admired. The video climbed to Bilibili's trending page the following day and quickly surpassed one million views, a result he later described as a "three-way win" in which the recommended creators gained attention, the audience received useful recommendations, and he himself discovered what resonated with viewers. That experience taught him a lesson that would shape his subsequent work: effective communication requires a "利他性," an orientation toward the audience's needs rather than the creator's self-expression. He subsequently produced six or seven more videos before settling on the creative direction that now defines his channel, a gradual process of refinement rather than a single moment of clarity.

What distinguishes Langhua Jiang from the crowded field of Chinese history content creators is his ability to make obscure, often overlooked aspects of the past feel immediately relevant and genuinely fascinating. His videos are organized around several recurring series. The "Chinese Encyclopedia History" series functions as a comprehensive guide to the daily lives of ancient Chinese people, covering topics ranging from clothing and food to the imperial examination system and funeral customs. The "Jianghu History" series explores the folk traditions and underworld stories of bandits, tomb raiders, and con artists that rarely appear in official historical narratives. The "Understanding Museums" series focuses on the artifacts and institutions that preserve China's material heritage. His content is characterized by a relaxed, conversational delivery that avoids academic jargon while still respecting the complexity of his subjects. He has described his approach as "thinning out" history, a metaphor that captures his method of extracting the most engaging and accessible elements from dense historical material without sacrificing accuracy. His videos are long by contemporary standards, often running twenty to thirty minutes, and he has explicitly rejected the pressure to conform to short-video conventions, a decision that has allowed him to build a dedicated audience willing to invest time in substantive content.

Among his most significant works is the 253-minute video "A Complete Tour of China's Top National Treasures in One Episode," released on June 1, 2025. The video surveys all 195 Chinese cultural relics that are prohibited from being taken abroad for exhibition, organized geographically and presented with the same accessible storytelling style that characterizes his shorter content. The production took nearly a year to complete, a period during which he maintained his regular weekly upload schedule simultaneously. The video was selected for Bilibili's "Weekly Must-Watch" list and has accumulated over 2.5 million views, an extraordinary figure for a four-hour history documentary. In an interview, Jiang explained that the project was a long-held personal ambition: he wanted viewers to be able to walk into any museum in China and encounter "familiar faces," artifacts whose stories they already knew. The video's success demonstrates that there is a substantial audience for deep, long-form historical content, even in an era dominated by short-form video. Other notable works include his video "How Did Ancient Chinese People Survive the Coldest Winters?" which accumulated over 2.5 million views within ten days of its release, and his "Chinese Surnames" series, which traces the origins of Chinese family names and has been widely shared among viewers interested in their own ancestral history.

Langhua Jiang's platform achievements reflect the growing prominence of knowledge content on Bilibili. His Bilibili follower count surpassed one million in June 2025, coinciding with the release of his national treasures video, and he has since grown to over three million followers across platforms. His "Chinese Encyclopedia History" series alone has accumulated 120 million views, while other series such as "Chinese Culinary History" and "Jianghu Strange Tales" have each reached tens of millions of views. In 2025, he published a book titled "An Illustrated Guide to Ancient Life and Culture," extending his work from video into print media. He has been recognized with Douyin's Annual Hardcore Content Award, and his videos have been cited in media outlets including The Paper and Southern Metropolis Daily as examples of the "new mass literature and art" movement, a cultural trend in which grassroots creators use digital platforms to make specialized knowledge accessible to general audiences.

The broader social value of Langhua Jiang's work lies in his demonstration that historical knowledge does not need to be simplified or sensationalized to reach a mass audience. He approaches history from the perspective of an ordinary person rather than an academic specialist, and he has argued that this outsider position is precisely what allows him to identify which aspects of the past will resonate with viewers who have no formal training in history. His videos encourage viewers to see history not as a collection of dates and names to be memorized but as a living resource for understanding human behavior, social organization, and cultural continuity. For young Chinese viewers who may feel disconnected from traditional culture, his work offers an accessible entry point that respects their intelligence while meeting them where they are. His emphasis on the "usefulness" of historical knowledge, not in a utilitarian sense but in the sense of enriching one's understanding of the present, aligns with Bilibili's broader mission to position itself as a platform where entertainment and education coexist.

In summary, Langhua Jiang represents a model of the creator as public storyteller, someone who uses digital media to bridge the gap between specialized knowledge and general curiosity. His decision to prioritize long-form, deeply researched content over algorithm-friendly short videos is a calculated risk that has paid off, both commercially and creatively. His background as a self-described "layperson" rather than a trained historian gives his work a relatability that more authoritative voices sometimes lack, while his commitment to accuracy and thorough research ensures that accessibility does not come at the expense of substance. For Bilibili, he is evidence that the platform's knowledge section can support creators who take intellectual risks and expect their audiences to follow. For the broader landscape of Chinese digital culture, he is a reminder that the most enduring content is often that which helps people understand themselves and their world a little better, one story at a time.

entry.title: Mianyang Liaoli: The Culinary Perfectionist Who Turned Recipe Videos into Literature
entry.summary: Mianyang Liaoli, whose real name is Zhang Yi, is a Chinese culinary content creator and one of the most respected figures in Bilibili's food section. A native of Changsha, Hunan Province, she previously worked in program production at Hunan Broadcasting System before founding her own…
entry.content:
Mianyang Liaoli, whose real name is Zhang Yi, is a Chinese culinary content creator and one of the most respected figures in Bilibili's food section. A native of Changsha, Hunan Province, she previously worked in program production at Hunan Broadcasting System before founding her own media company, Changsha Chi Bu Pang Culture Media Co., Ltd. Since uploading her first video, a demonstration of cheese balls inspired by a Hokkaido curry restaurant, on December 22, 2015, she has built one of the most durable careers in Chinese food media, accumulating over 11.9 million followers on Bilibili and more than 86 million total likes as of January 2026.Her channel's name, which translates to "Sheep Cuisine," is a whimsical self-reference, but the work itself is anything but casual. Mianyang Liaoli approaches cooking with the rigor of a researcher and the sensibility of a writer, and in doing so, she has redefined what a food video can be.

Her path into content creation was, by her own account, largely accidental. In a 2022 interview, she explained that she began filming simply to document her kitchen life, and her first upload unexpectedly appeared on Bilibili's homepage, which encouraged her to continue.Her early videos reflected her background in television production: they were slow-paced, gentle, and instructional, closer in spirit to a televised cooking program than to the rapidly edited, personality-driven content that would later dominate the platform. She soon recognized that this style did not suit her temperament. "That overly televised, slow-paced format didn't really match my personality," she recalled, "so I gradually added some popular memes and some absurdist elements."The turning point came when she produced a sponsored video and, worried that the advertisement would feel intrusive, deliberately accelerated the pacing and adopted a style she describes as "deadpan nonsense." The result was a revelation: she had found a voice that was simultaneously irreverent and meticulous, and from that point forward, her videos became exercises in controlled chaos.

What distinguishes Mianyang Liaoli from the crowded field of Chinese food creators is the unusual combination of technical ambition, narrative craft, and linguistic playfulness that defines her work. Her most celebrated videos involve attempts to recreate dishes of extraordinary difficulty: royal recipes from the Qing dynasty, molecular gastronomy showpieces, regional specialties that require days of preparation, and dishes from animated films and video games. The complexity is genuine; she has spent weeks researching and testing a single recipe, and her willingness to document failure alongside success gives her videos an emotional arc that pure instructional content lacks.Her editing style is brisk and densely layered, with quick cuts, sound effects, and visual gags that reward repeat viewing. But her most distinctive signature is her narration. Mianyang Liaoli writes rhyming, rhythmic voice-over scripts that have earned her the official designation of "the rhyming maniac of the culinary world."Her descriptions of food are not merely functional; they are literary. A bowl of clear chicken broth becomes "a mirror-still lake at dawn, unrippled and serene, until a sudden drift of rich, intoxicating savor sends shimmering waves across its glassy surface."Fans have taken to imitating her style in the comments, turning her video sections into impromptu poetry competitions.

Among her most influential works is "Dragon's Chant Strawberry," a recreation of a legendary molecular gastronomy dessert that requires cooking a strawberry through a temperature range spanning from minus 196 degrees Celsius to 99 degrees Celsius.The video became a viral phenomenon, accumulating over 2.35 million likes on Douyin and spawning a wave of imitation attempts across Chinese social media.Her "Sheep's Howl Strawberry," a playful response to her own success, transformed the original concept into a square-shaped confection, demonstrating her ability to build on her own creative output with humor and self-awareness. Other signature videos include her recreation of a Qing imperial recipe that involves stuffing meat into bean sprouts, her attempt to make Indian flatbread and bamboo-pressed noodles at home, and her series of "survival cuisine" tutorials designed for viewers with limited cooking skills and time.Her 2025 original program featuring an AI-designed "interstellar meteorite fried chicken" extended her experimentation into the intersection of artificial intelligence and cooking.The structural variety of her channel, organized around three distinct pillars of elaborate recipe recreation, city food exploration vlogs, and beginner-friendly survival cooking, allows her to serve audiences with vastly different needs while maintaining a coherent creative identity.

Mianyang Liaoli's platform achievements are substantial. She has been selected for Bilibili's Top 100 UP Creators list for six consecutive years, from 2019 through 2024, a distinction that places her among the platform's most consistently recognized creators.Her average video performance is remarkable: her works routinely exceed one million views, with her top videos reaching approximately 16.5 million, 12 million, and 10 million plays respectively.Her fan engagement metrics are equally impressive, with an average of 392,000 likes and 246,000 coin-tips per video, and a follower-to-view ratio approaching sixty percent, indicating that her audience consists largely of dedicated subscribers rather than casual viewers.Beyond Bilibili, she maintains a significant presence on YouTube under the channel name Sheep HoHo, where she has accumulated over 800,000 subscribers, and her total cross-platform following exceeds twenty million.In 2026, she was appointed Chief Content Co-Creation Officer for the 48th World Skills Competition, a role that recognized her ability to communicate the value of craftsmanship to a broad public audience. At the competition's 100-day countdown event, she spoke about her experiences with intangible cultural heritage techniques and traditional snacks, from sugar figurine blowing to bamboo-pressed noodles and Beijing roast duck, observing that only by personally attempting these crafts can one understand the meaning of "one minute on stage, ten years of practice offstage."

The broader social significance of Mianyang Liaoli's work lies in her elevation of cooking from a domestic chore to a subject worthy of intellectual and artistic seriousness. By treating recipes as research projects and food writing as literature, she has helped legitimize culinary content as a form of knowledge production rather than mere entertainment. Her exploration of intangible cultural heritage foods, including her collaborations with traditional craftspeople and her participation in World Skills initiatives, positions her as a bridge between contemporary digital culture and the preservation of artisanal knowledge.For younger viewers who may never attempt her most complex recipes, her videos offer something equally valuable: a model of how to approach any skill with patience, curiosity, and a willingness to fail publicly and try again. Her emphasis on documenting the full process, including the failures and frustrations, rather than presenting only polished results, aligns with Bilibili's broader culture of authentic, process-oriented content and distinguishes her from creators who prioritize visual perfection over genuine instruction.

In summary, Mianyang Liaoli represents a rare synthesis of artistic ambition and audience accessibility. She has built a career on the conviction that cooking is worth taking seriously, not in the sense of solemnity, but in the sense of investing genuine effort, thought, and creativity into every dish. Her rhyming narration, her willingness to spend weeks on a single recipe, and her refusal to condescend to her audience by simplifying the complexity of her subject have earned her a level of loyalty and respect that few food creators achieve. For Bilibili, she is a cornerstone of the platform's food section and a demonstration that knowledge content can be beautiful, funny, and deeply personal. For viewers around the world, she offers a window into Chinese culinary culture that is neither exoticized nor oversimplified, but presented with the care and precision of a craftsperson who believes that the best way to honor a tradition is to attempt it yourself, however imperfectly.

entry.title: GenJi: The Digital Educator Who Built a Million-Strong Classroom on Bilibili
entry.summary: GenJi, whose real name is Li Genji, is a Chinese digital education creator and one of the most prominent figures in Bilibili's knowledge section. Operating under the account name "GenJi Really Wants to Teach You" (GenJi Shi Zhen Xiang Jiao Hui Ni), he has built…
entry.content:
GenJi, whose real name is Li Genji, is a Chinese digital education creator and one of the most prominent figures in Bilibili's knowledge section. Operating under the account name "GenJi Really Wants to Teach You" (GenJi Shi Zhen Xiang Jiao Hui Ni), he has built a following of over ten million users on Bilibili, making him one of the platform's most-followed educational creators. His rise from a university student offering free lectures in borrowed classrooms to a nationally recognized UP creator is a story about the convergence of technical skill, pedagogical conviction, and the expanding reach of China's online knowledge economy. In January 2026, he was named to Bilibili's annual Top 100 UP Creators list, a distinction that confirmed his status not merely as a popular account but as a defining voice in the platform's educational ecosystem.

Li Genji's path into teaching began long before he ever opened a video editing program. As a primary school student, he was already the classmate others turned to for help with difficult problems, a role he describes as his first experience of explaining complex ideas to peers. That instinct followed him into university, where he developed a rare combination of design, programming, and product development skills. He became proficient in front-end and back-end development as well as visual interaction design, and by his early undergraduate years he was already serving as the youngest lecturer at his institution. It was during this period that he identified a disconnect that would shape the rest of his career: many university graduates struggled to find employment not because they lacked intelligence or effort, but because the skills taught in classrooms had little direct application to the demands of the professional world. The gap between what students were learning and what employers actually needed became the problem he set out to solve.

His response was to begin offering free public lectures across universities in central China, covering topics ranging from design tools to programming techniques. The lectures were practical by design, focused on skills that students could immediately apply rather than abstract theory. He continued this practice for nearly a decade, preparing course materials, coordinating venues, and teaching without any financial compensation. The work was demanding and often invisible, but the feedback he received from students who landed jobs or completed difficult graduation projects using what they had learned convinced him that the effort was worthwhile. He founded a student organization called Cloud Workshop (Yunding Zuofang), whose logo, a ladder stretching into the clouds, symbolized his belief that knowledge should function as a ladder for upward mobility. That logo remains on his Bilibili avatar today, a small but telling marker of continuity between his early volunteer teaching and his current platform career.

The transition from offline lectures to online video creation came in 2020, when the pandemic forced him to pause his in-person classes. Rather than abandon the work, he began recording the same practical lessons he had been delivering in person and uploading them to Bilibili. His first upload, a Photoshop tutorial recorded without elaborate production values or scripted performance, accumulated over 1.42 million views. The success was not the result of algorithmic luck but of a simple insight: learners wanted instruction that felt like a real classroom, not a polished entertainment product. GenJi's videos retain that classroom quality. They are structured, patient, and grounded in the assumption that the viewer is genuinely there to learn something useful. His speaking style is direct and unadorned, and his editing favors clarity over spectacle, a deliberate choice that distinguishes him from creators who prioritize production value over instructional substance.

As his audience grew, GenJi expanded his subject matter from design and programming into artificial intelligence, a shift that aligned both with his own technical interests and with the broader cultural moment. His AI-related content explains machine learning concepts, demonstrates practical applications of AI tools, and addresses the anxieties many learners feel about automation and job displacement. He approaches AI not as a distant technological marvel but as a set of tools that ordinary people can learn to use, a framing that has resonated with students, career-changers, and professionals seeking to remain relevant in a rapidly changing economy. His teaching philosophy, which he summarizes as "really wanting to teach you," is embedded in his account name and functions as both a promise to his audience and a standard against which he measures his own work. The phrase captures his rejection of performative education, the kind of content that gestures at learning without delivering it.

The scale of GenJi's platform presence reflects the demand for this kind of instruction. His account has surpassed ten million followers on Bilibili, placing him among the platform's most-subscribed individual creators. He has been featured in Chinese media, including a profile in Youth Daily that traced his evolution from a primary school helper to a digital education pioneer, and his selection for the 2025 Bilibili Top 100 UP Creators list placed him alongside figures like Luo Xiang and Lao Fanqie as one of the platform's defining creators. His influence extends beyond his own channel: he has built a broader educational ecosystem that includes self-developed intelligent hardware and a suite of learning resources designed to make technical skills accessible to users who may not have formal training in computer science. The Cloud Workshop logo on his avatar is a reminder that his project began as a voluntary effort to share knowledge, not as a commercial enterprise, and that the values informing his current work remain rooted in that origin.

The social value of GenJi's work lies in his demonstration that digital platforms can function as genuine educational infrastructure rather than merely as entertainment distribution networks. Bilibili's knowledge section emerged as a significant content category in the late 2010s and early 2020s, and creators like GenJi have been central to its legitimacy. By offering rigorous, practical instruction at no cost to anyone with an internet connection, he has contributed to a broader shift in how Chinese young people think about learning, career preparation, and the relationship between formal education and self-directed study. His emphasis on "knowledge universalization" (zhishi puhui) reflects a conviction that access to practical skills should not be determined by institutional affiliation or economic capacity. For viewers who cannot afford expensive training programs or who live far from major educational centers, his videos offer a pathway to competence that would otherwise be unavailable.

In summary, GenJi represents a model of the creator as educator, someone who treats the platform not as a stage for self-promotion but as a classroom that can accommodate millions of students simultaneously. His decade of unpaid public teaching before his online success is not merely a biographical detail but the foundation of his credibility: he earned his audience by helping people learn, not by chasing trends. His expansion into AI education reflects an awareness that the skills people need are changing, and his willingness to adapt his teaching to new technologies without abandoning his commitment to practical usefulness suggests that his influence will remain relevant as the educational landscape continues to evolve. For Bilibili, he is evidence that the platform's knowledge ambitions are not aspirational rhetoric but measurable reality. For learners, he is a reminder that the most valuable educational content is often the least flashy, and that a teacher who genuinely wants to teach is worth more than a thousand polished performances.

entry.title: Papi Jiang: The First Lady of Chinese Internet Comedy and Her Decade-Long Reinvention
entry.summary: Papi Jiang, born Jiang Yilei on February 17, 1987, in Shanghai, is a Chinese actress, short-video creator, and one of the most enduring figures in the history of Chinese internet culture. She graduated from the Central Academy of Drama with both a bachelor's and a…
entry.content:
Papi Jiang, born Jiang Yilei on February 17, 1987, in Shanghai, is a Chinese actress, short-video creator, and one of the most enduring figures in the history of Chinese internet culture. She graduated from the Central Academy of Drama with both a bachelor's and a master's degree in directing, a background that distinguishes her from the vast majority of Chinese content creators who entered the field without formal training in performance or narrative construction. Her channel on Bilibili, where she is officially certified as a "2018 Top 100 UP Creator" and a "Renowned Comedy UP Creator," has accumulated over 9.4 million followers and more than 1.29 billion total views as of September 2026. But her significance extends far beyond any single platform metric. Papi Jiang is widely credited with legitimizing short-form comedy as a serious creative discipline in China, and her career trajectory, from a graduate student posting videos from her dormitory to a producer overseeing a content studio, offers a case study in how a creator can survive and thrive across multiple cycles of platform evolution.

Papi Jiang's path to internet fame was neither linear nor accidental. She grew up in Shanghai and attended the Shanghai No. 3 Girls' High School, where her saxophone talent in the school's girls' wind band earned her a twenty-point bonus on her high school entrance examination and a guaranteed place in the school's high school division. She was accepted into the Central Academy of Drama's directing program in 2005 and spent her undergraduate years actively involved in theater, both performing in and directing stage productions. After graduation, she explored several professional directions without finding a stable footing, and in 2013, at the age of twenty-six, she made the deliberate decision to return to the Central Academy of Drama for a master's degree in directing. It was during this period of graduate study that she began uploading short comedic videos to Chinese social media platforms, initially as a creative outlet rather than a career strategy. Her breakout came in 2015 and 2016, when a series of videos featuring her signature technique of accelerated voice modulation, rapid costume changes, and sharp observational humor about everyday life went viral across Weibo, WeChat, and Bilibili. By March 2016, she was being described by Chinese media as the "number one internet celebrity of 2016," and her account had attracted millions of followers within a matter of months.

What made Papi Jiang's content distinctive was not merely its humor but its structural sophistication. Unlike the loose, improvisational style that characterized much of Chinese short-form comedy at the time, her videos were tightly scripted, carefully paced, and built around a clear comedic premise that she would explore through multiple character perspectives. In a typical early video, she might play five or six different roles, each representing a recognizable social archetype—the anxious mother, the dismissive boyfriend, the overly competitive colleague—and use rapid cuts and voice changes to create the illusion of a conversation among them. This multi-role technique, combined with her background in directing, gave her videos a theatrical quality that set them apart from the confessional, talking-head format that dominated the platform. Her dialogue was colloquial and often self-deprecating, drawing on the anxieties and absurdities of urban Chinese life: the pressures of marriage and childbearing, the indignities of office politics, the gap between aspirational consumer culture and financial reality. She described herself in her videos with the now-iconic tagline, "I am Papi Jiang, a woman who combines beauty and talent," a line delivered with enough ironic distance to signal that she was fully aware of the absurdity of self-branding in the attention economy.

The commercial and cultural impact of Papi Jiang's early success was unprecedented. In March 2016, she received 12 million yuan in first-round financing from ZhenFund, Logic Show, and two other investment firms, with an estimated valuation of approximately 120 million yuan, making her the first internet celebrity in China to receive venture capital investment. In April of that year, the first commercial placement on one of her videos was auctioned for 22 million yuan, a figure that shocked observers and signaled that short-form video could be a viable advertising medium at scale. This auction is widely regarded as a watershed moment in the professionalization of Chinese content creation, demonstrating that individual creators could command advertising rates comparable to traditional media. In 2018, she was named to Bilibili's inaugural Top 100 UP Creators list, and in the same year, she was appointed Chief Content Officer of Baidu App, a role that placed her at the intersection of content creation and platform strategy. She also co-founded papitube, a multi-channel network focused on incubating and managing short-video creators, which at its peak represented dozens of signed talents and was recognized as one of China's leading MCN organizations.

Papi Jiang's creative output has evolved substantially over the past decade. In the late 2010s and early 2020s, she expanded into acting, appearing in films such as "The Truth About Beauty" and "Wish You Were Here," and taking a supporting role in Wong Kar-wai's acclaimed television series "Blossoms Shanghai," where she played Ling Hong, a boutique owner whose pragmatic, street-smart personality provided a counterpoint to the more romantic protagonists. Her performance was widely praised for its naturalism and comic timing, with critics noting that her background in directing gave her a nuanced understanding of how to build a character within an ensemble. In 2024, she made a significant structural decision: she stepped back from her management role at papitube and returned to full-time content creation, launching a new interview program called "Warm Welcome." The show's format is deliberately minimalist—one table, two chairs, no elaborate sets or scripted segments—and it centers on guests sharing personal recommendations for everyday products while engaging in unguarded conversation. The program became a breakout success, with over 70 million views on Bilibili and 300 million on Douyin, and it was credited with revitalizing the careers of several established entertainers who appeared as guests.

The broader significance of Papi Jiang's career lies in her demonstration that creative longevity on Chinese social media is possible through continuous reinvention rather than mere consistency. She has outlasted the vast majority of her contemporaries from the 2016 "internet celebrity" boom, many of whom faded within a few years. Her ability to move from short-form comedy to acting to interview-based content reflects a willingness to abandon formats that no longer serve her and to invest in new creative challenges even when the commercial incentives favor sticking with proven formulas. For Bilibili, she represents an early bridge between the platform's niche gaming and anime origins and its later emergence as a mainstream cultural force. For aspiring creators, her career demonstrates that a formal education in narrative craft can translate into meaningful advantages in a field that often valorizes spontaneity over discipline. And for the broader landscape of Chinese digital culture, she stands as a reminder that the most durable figures are not those who chase every trend but those who build a body of work that can accommodate growth and change.

In summary, Papi Jiang is not merely a successful content creator but a transitional figure who helped define what Chinese short-form video could be and then repeatedly redefined what her own career could become. Her decade-long presence at the center of Chinese internet culture is a testament to her creative instincts, her willingness to evolve, and her insistence on maintaining a degree of artistic control even as the commercial pressures around her intensified. She remains, in the most literal sense of her own famous tagline, a woman who combines beauty and talent—but more importantly, she combines talent with the discipline and adaptability required to sustain a creative life over the long term.

entry.title: He Tongxue: The Tech Storyteller Who Redefined Digital Creativity on Bilibili
entry.summary: He Tongxue, whose real name is He Shijie, is a Chinese digital technology content creator and one of the most influential figures in Bilibili's technology and knowledge ecosystem. Born in Taiyuan, Shanxi Province, he graduated from the International School of Beijing University of Posts and…
entry.content:
He Tongxue, whose real name is He Shijie, is a Chinese digital technology content creator and one of the most influential figures in Bilibili's technology and knowledge ecosystem. Born in Taiyuan, Shanxi Province, he graduated from the International School of Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, where he studied telecommunications engineering with a focus on internet of things technology. His channel, "Teacher, My Name Is He Tongxue," which translates roughly to "Teacher, I Am He Tongxue," is a deliberate play on the classroom roll-call convention, signaling from the outset his identity as a student creator speaking to a peer audience. He began uploading videos to Bilibili in October 2017, with his first upload being a simple Premiere tutorial on creating a "door transition" effect. What began as a modest hobby while he was still a university student would, within two years, transform him into a national phenomenon, and within a decade, into a creator with over twelve million followers on Bilibili and a significant international presence through his English-language YouTube channel, HTX Studio.

He Tongxue's entry into content creation was driven less by a desire for fame than by a genuine fascination with how technology works and how it can be explained to ordinary people. His early videos were characterized by a distinctive blend of technical curiosity, cinematic storytelling, and emotional resonance, a combination that set him apart from the conventional tech review format that dominated Bilibili's technology section at the time. Rather than simply listing specifications or benchmarking hardware, he approached each video as a narrative about technology's place in human life, often using himself as the protagonist in a story of experimentation, failure, and eventual discovery. This storytelling instinct, combined with a meticulous attention to visual composition and sound design, gave his work a production quality that rivaled professional media while retaining the intimacy and authenticity of a personal vlog.

The video that launched He Tongxue into mainstream visibility was his June 2019 upload titled "How Fast Is 5G Really?" The video, released just as China was beginning its large-scale rollout of 5G networks, approached the question not through abstract technical explanation but through a series of vivid, relatable experiments. He tested 5G speeds in locations ranging from a university campus to a tourist landmark, measured the latency in scenarios that mattered to ordinary users, and ultimately posed a deeper question: what will 5G actually enable that 4G cannot? The video resonated because it captured a moment of collective curiosity about a technology that was being heavily promoted but poorly understood. It accumulated tens of millions of views, was widely shared across Chinese social media, and established He Tongxue as a creator capable of translating complex technological shifts into compelling human narratives.

What distinguishes He Tongxue from other technology creators on Bilibili is the extent to which his videos function as short films rather than conventional product reviews. His 2021 video "I Made the Product Apple Gave Up On" documented his attempt to build a functional version of AirPower, Apple's cancelled wireless charging mat, using a combination of off-the-shelf components, custom 3D-printed parts, and a significant amount of trial and error. The video was not merely a demonstration of technical skill; it was a meditation on the nature of innovation, the value of pursuing seemingly impossible projects, and the emotional payoff of bringing an idea into physical reality. In 2025, his video "We Made a Special Keyboard" documented his team's effort to design and build a single-handed keyboard for a user with a disability, a project that combined engineering problem-solving with genuine social purpose. That video won Bilibili's Annual Best Work award, recognizing both its technical ambition and its humanitarian impulse.

He Tongxue's platform influence is substantial and measurable. As of January 2026, his Bilibili channel has over 12.56 million followers, placing him among the platform's most-followed individual creators. He has been selected for Bilibili's Top 100 UP Creators list in multiple years, including 2021, 2023, and 2025, and his videos consistently achieve millions of views. His interview with Apple CEO Tim Cook in February 2021, conducted remotely during the COVID-19 pandemic, was a landmark moment for Bilibili as a platform, demonstrating that its creators could secure access to global technology leaders on terms of intellectual equality. In 2024, he was named to Forbes China's 50 New Media Opinion Leaders list, and he participated in the documentary "Yang Sheng," which explored the intersection of technology and personal life. His expansion to YouTube under the HTX Studio brand, where he gained over one million subscribers within a year, represents a rare instance of a Chinese creator achieving significant traction in the English-language digital sphere.

The broader social value of He Tongxue's work lies in his demonstration that technology content can be both intellectually rigorous and emotionally engaging. He does not shy away from technical detail, but he always frames it within a human story. His videos encourage viewers to see technology not as a collection of inert objects but as a domain of possibility, creativity, and ethical choice. For young viewers considering careers in engineering, design, or media, he offers a model of creative practice that is both commercially viable and personally meaningful. His willingness to address controversial topics, including a 2025 incident involving a ride-hailing driver that sparked debate about creator responsibility, and his subsequent public apology and disclosure of his company's financial challenges, added a dimension of vulnerability and accountability that is rare among high-profile creators. This willingness to engage with failure and criticism, rather than retreating into a curated public image, has arguably deepened his credibility with his audience.

In summary, He Tongxue represents a distinctive model of the creator as auteur, someone who treats each video as a work of authored storytelling rather than a content product. His background in engineering gives him the technical fluency to attempt ambitious projects, while his instincts as a filmmaker give him the ability to communicate why those projects matter. For Bilibili, he is a symbol of the platform's capacity to nurture creators who transcend their original niche and speak to a broad national and international audience. For the broader landscape of technology media, he is a reminder that the most enduring stories about technology are not about specifications but about people, their curiosity, their limitations, and their capacity to imagine and build a better version of the world around them.

entry.title: Lao Fanqie: The Gamer Who Became Bilibili's First Ten-Million-Follower Creator
entry.summary: Lao Fanqie, whose real name is Zhang Qiushi, is a Chinese video creator, game commentator, and one of the most influential figures in the history of Bilibili, China's premier video-sharing platform for user-generated content. Born on August 13, 1997, in Inner Mongolia and raised in…
entry.content:
Lao Fanqie, whose real name is Zhang Qiushi, is a Chinese video creator, game commentator, and one of the most influential figures in the history of Bilibili, China's premier video-sharing platform for user-generated content. Born on August 13, 1997, in Inner Mongolia and raised in Shanghai, he is a graduate of Fudan University, where he earned a master's degree in finance after completing his undergraduate studies in the university's economics program. His academic achievements at Fudan were notable: he received a freshman scholarship, maintained a GPA of 3.94 during his junior year, and graduated in the top ten percent of his class, which secured him a recommendation for graduate study without the need for entrance examinations. Despite this conventional path of academic excellence, Lao Fanqie's true passion lay in video creation, a pursuit he began in middle school when he first explored the basic video editing software pre-installed on his family computer. What started as a classroom assignment evolved into a decade-long creative journey that would ultimately redefine what was possible for individual content creators on Bilibili.

Lao Fanqie's entry into Bilibili came in 2013, when he uploaded a Pokémon gameplay commentary video that rapidly climbed to the third position on the platform's daily viewership chart. At the time, he was still a high school student, and his parents had restricted his computer use to academic purposes only. Undeterred, he engaged in what he later described as "underground creation," producing videos in secret while maintaining his studies. By the time he entered university, he had already accumulated three to four hundred thousand followers on the platform. His channel's positioning has always been rooted in game commentary, but his creative output has expanded to encompass music, short films, and reality programming, reflecting a restless creative energy that refuses to be confined to a single genre. As of March 2026, his Bilibili channel has over twenty million followers, and his cumulative video views exceed 3.48 billion, making him one of the most-watched individual creators in the platform's history.

What distinguishes Lao Fanqie from other gaming creators is his distinctive approach to narrative construction and comedic timing. Rather than simply playing games and offering live commentary, he treats his videos as carefully scripted short films, often transforming open-world games such as Grand Theft Auto and Minecraft into structured comedic narratives with clear beginnings, developments, and resolutions. His editing style is fast-paced and densely layered, with rapid cuts, sound effects, and visual gags that reward attentive viewing. His voice-over delivery is similarly brisk, a characteristic that interviewers have noted extends even to his English speech, leading some commentators to joke that listening to him is like taking an English listening comprehension examination. The humor in his videos is often self-deprecating and absurdist, drawing on internet culture and gaming conventions while remaining accessible to viewers who may not be familiar with the specific games he features. This combination of technical polish, narrative ambition, and genuine comedic talent has created a viewing experience that feels more like watching a well-produced web series than a conventional gameplay video.

Several of Lao Fanqie's video series have achieved iconic status within Bilibili's gaming community. His "Shishang Zui Sao" series, which translates roughly to "The Most Ridiculous" or "The Most Outrageous," includes installments focused on games such as Hitman, Red Dead Redemption, and Batman, each featuring elaborate scenarios that showcase his characteristically irreverent approach to gameplay. The "Zhao Si Da's Fantasy Adventure" series and "Hardcore Black Uncle Fights Zombies," based on The Walking Dead, further demonstrate his ability to impose coherent narrative structures on disparate gaming experiences. One of his most celebrated works, "Six Rogues," released in October 2016, represents a departure from gameplay content into pure short-film territory, and it remains a landmark in his creative evolution. In 2018, he won the second season of Story Man, a competitive storytelling program on Bilibili, which confirmed his reputation as not merely a gamer but a genuine entertainer and narrative talent. His 2020 reality show "Happy Brothers," co-starring several other prominent Bilibili creators, extended his reach beyond gaming into mainstream entertainment.

The platform impact of Lao Fanqie is difficult to overstate. In April 2020, he became the first individual creator in Bilibili's history to surpass ten million followers, a milestone that was widely reported in Chinese media, including by People's Daily and China Youth Daily. He has been named to Bilibili's Top 100 UP Creators list for eight consecutive years, from 2018 through 2025, a distinction shared by only a handful of creators. His total view count of over 3.48 billion places him among the platform's most-watched accounts, and his follower count of more than twenty million as of early 2026 continues to grow steadily. Beyond these quantitative measures, he has received the platform's Highest Popularity Award and has been recognized for his commercial influence, reflecting his ability to translate creative success into sustainable professional practice. In 2021, he was selected as a lead instructor for the "Youth Great Learning" online ideological education program, a role typically reserved for figures of significant cultural standing, and in 2026 he was appointed as the Chief Content Co-Creation Officer for the 48th World Skills Competition, further demonstrating his crossover appeal into institutional and educational contexts.

The broader social value of Lao Fanqie's work lies in his demonstration that gaming content can be intellectually substantial and creatively ambitious. By combining rigorous academic achievement at one of China's most prestigious universities with a full-time career as a video creator, he has challenged the persistent stereotype that gaming and internet content creation are incompatible with serious intellectual pursuits. His videos are not merely entertainment products but constructed narratives that display a sophisticated understanding of storytelling, pacing, and audience engagement. For young viewers who aspire to creative careers, he represents a model of professionalization that does not require abandoning intellectual curiosity or academic discipline. At the same time, his sustained success over more than a decade reflects the maturation of Bilibili's creator ecosystem, in which individual talents can build durable careers and evolve their craft over time. His journey from a middle school student secretly editing videos on a family computer to the platform's first ten-million-follower creator is a testament to both his personal dedication and the cultural shift that has made gaming content a legitimate and respected form of creative expression in contemporary China.

In summary, Lao Fanqie occupies a unique position in the landscape of Chinese digital culture. He is simultaneously a product of and a catalyst for the transformation of Bilibili from a niche anime-focused community into a broad-based entertainment and knowledge platform. His creative evolution, from Pokémon commentary to scripted comedic short films, mirrors the platform's own expansion and diversification. His academic credentials, far from being incidental to his success, inform the discipline and narrative intelligence that distinguish his best work. For English-speaking readers who may be unfamiliar with Bilibili, Lao Fanqie offers a compelling entry point into understanding how gaming content, internet culture, and youth identity intersect in the Chinese digital sphere. His enduring significance lies not only in the millions of followers he has attracted but in the standard of creative excellence he has set for a generation of content creators who see in his work the possibility of building something both personally meaningful and widely resonant.

entry.title: Luo Xiang: The Legal Scholar Who Made Criminal Law a Viral Sensation on Bilibili
entry.summary: Luo Xiang is a Chinese jurist, law professor, and one of the most recognizable public intellectuals on Bilibili, China’s leading video-sharing platform. Born in 1977 in Leiyang, Hunan Province, he serves as a professor of law and director of the Institute of Criminal Law at…
entry.content:
Luo Xiang is a Chinese jurist, law professor, and one of the most recognizable public intellectuals on Bilibili, China’s leading video-sharing platform. Born in 1977 in Leiyang, Hunan Province, he serves as a professor of law and director of the Institute of Criminal Law at the China University of Political Science and Law (CUPL). His academic credentials include a bachelor’s degree from the China Youth University of Political Studies, a master’s degree in criminal law from CUPL, and a doctoral degree in criminal law from Peking University Law School. He also spent time as a visiting scholar at Duke University in the United States between 2013 and 2014. While his formal career has been rooted in legal academia, it was an unexpected foray into online video that transformed him into a household name among Chinese young people. In March 2020, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, Luo was invited to join Bilibili. Within two days of creating his account, “Luo Xiang Talks Criminal Law,” he had amassed over one million followers; within six months, that number surpassed ten million. His channel quickly became a cultural phenomenon, blending rigorous legal education with narrative flair and a distinctive comic timing that resonated far beyond law students.

What sets Luo Xiang apart from conventional legal educators is his extraordinary ability to make abstract legal doctrines vivid, memorable, and even entertaining. His lectures typically revolve around hypothetical criminal scenarios featuring a recurring fictional character named Zhang San, a figure so notoriously versatile in his wrongdoing that he has been dubbed the “outlaw Zhang San” by fans. In Luo’s hands, Zhang San might commit theft, fraud, assault, or even bizarre crimes involving panda poaching or accidental death through ill-conceived gifts, each scenario carefully constructed to illustrate a specific legal principle. The humor is never gratuitous; it serves as a pedagogical device that lowers the barrier to entry for complex criminal law concepts. Luo’s speaking style is deliberate and measured, often punctuated by deadpan observations and philosophical asides that invite viewers to reflect on the moral dimensions of law. His videos are not heavily edited or visually flashy, relying instead on the strength of his narration and the intellectual energy he brings to each case. This minimalist production aesthetic, combined with his professorial authority, creates a distinctive viewing experience that feels both educational and intimate, as though one is sitting in on a particularly engaging university seminar.

Several of Luo’s video series and individual lectures have achieved exceptional popularity and cultural penetration. His early Bilibili uploads, which were essentially recordings of his law examination preparation courses, rapidly accumulated millions of views and hundreds of thousands of likes. One widely shared clip involves a hypothetical case in which a man buys a hundred bungee-jumping tickets for someone he resents, and the recipient dies on the ninety-ninth jump; Luo uses this absurd scenario to explore the boundaries of harmful conduct and causation in criminal law. Another beloved example features a college student named Zhang San who fails his CET-4 English exam and then purchases a forged diploma from a top university, leading Luo into a nuanced discussion of forgery offenses and the distinction between administrative and criminal liability. The “Zhang San” character has become so iconic that fans have collectively compiled an elaborate fictional biography of his criminal exploits, turning him into a meme-like figure within Bilibili’s knowledge community. Luo’s most-viewed content typically combines these memorable case studies with broader reflections on justice, punishment, and the rule of law, drawing viewers who may have no intention of ever practicing law but are captivated by the intellectual rigor and ethical inquiry on display.

By any measure, Luo Xiang’s platform influence is remarkable. As of early 2026, his Bilibili channel has over 32 million followers, making him one of the most followed accounts on the entire platform. He has been selected for Bilibili’s annual “Top 100 UP Creators” list for six consecutive years since 2020, a testament to his sustained relevance and consistent output quality. In 2020, he received the platform’s “Most Popular UP Creator” award, and in December of that year, he was named one of China Central Television’s “Annual Figures in the Rule of Law” for his contributions to public legal education. The following year, China Newsweek also recognized him as an annual figure in the rule of law. His reach extends beyond Bilibili: his lectures circulate widely on other social media platforms, and his books, including “The Details of the Rule of Law,” “Criminal Law Lectures,” and “The Circle of Justice,” have found a substantial general readership. In 2024, he was appointed as an adjunct professor at Shandong University, further cementing his status as a bridge between academic law and public discourse.

The broader social value of Luo Xiang’s work lies in his transformation of legal education from an elite, examination-oriented pursuit into a form of accessible public culture. Bilibili’s knowledge section, where his channel is situated, emerged as a major content category only around 2019–2020, and Luo’s success helped legitimize and popularize the idea that serious intellectual content could thrive on a platform otherwise associated with gaming, anime, and entertainment. His lectures encourage viewers to think critically about justice, human dignity, and the limits of state power, often weaving in references to classical philosophy and literature. For a generation of Chinese young people navigating a complex legal and social landscape, Luo offers not only information but also a vocabulary for ethical reasoning. At the same time, his approach has not been without criticism; some observers have suggested that his idealism may at times oversimplify the practical realities of legal practice, and he has faced occasional controversies over misattributed statements circulated online in his name. Nevertheless, the dominant assessment of his impact is positive, with scholars and media commentators crediting him with opening a new model for legal communication in the digital age.

In summary, Luo Xiang represents a rare convergence of academic rigor, pedagogical creativity, and platform-native communication. He did not set out to become an internet celebrity; his initial foray into online video was an extension of his longstanding commitment to teaching. Yet the scale of his reach has made him a central figure in China’s evolving landscape of public knowledge. His enduring significance lies not merely in the millions of views his lectures attract, but in the way he has demonstrated that complex, serious subjects can find a broad and eager audience when presented with clarity, humor, and genuine intellectual passion. For Bilibili, he is a symbol of the platform’s aspiration to be more than entertainment; for legal education, he is a reminder that the law belongs to everyone, not just to specialists; and for his viewers, he is a teacher in the truest sense, one who makes the pursuit of understanding feel both urgent and joyful.
